item.title: Ultraslow diffusion emerging from local symmetry breaking in quenched disorder
item.description: arXiv:2611.00831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many dynamical systems operate in disordered environments. In this Letter, we investigate how quenched randomness modifies particle diffusion. We show that, in finite-strength potential landscapes, low disorder densities can induce logarithmically ultraslow diffusion. The underlying mechanism originates from local symmetry breaking in particular potential configurations: Barrier-well structures form directional channels, causing particles to undergo hierarchical capture, escape, and recapture processes. A coarse-grained channel theory yields an approximate scaling prediction for the mean-square displacement. Counterintuitively, when the disorder density reaches the fully disordered limit, the system returns to normal diffusion, revealing a nontrivial, nonmonotonic relationship between disorder density and transport type. This mechanism is observed in both nonlinear maps and stochastic systems.
item.dc:creator: Jin Liu, Rainer Klages, Huihai Wang, Kehui Sun

item.title: PRISM: Unifying multiphysics optothermal transport and identifiability-guided inference for nanoscale thermal metrology
item.description: arXiv:2611.02475v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantifying thermal transport across micro- and nanoscale heterostructures is critical for solid-state devices and relies on fitting heat-transfer models to thermal-wave spectra. When probing scales approach optical absorption depths, electron-phonon equilibration lengths, or phonon mean free paths, classical surface-heating Fourier models can match measured phase spectra while returning biased, measurement-dependent parameters. Here we introduce PRISM (Physics-Resolved Inference and Screening Meta-framework), an agentic framework coupling multilayer optical transfer-matrix electrodynamics, two-temperature electron-phonon relaxation, and nonlocal Guyer-Krumhansl phonon hydrodynamics within a unified admittance formalism, paired with singular-value-decomposition identifiability screening and knowledge-guided routing. Demonstrated with frequency-domain thermoreflectance across stacks relevant to microelectronic contacts and dielectric barriers, PRISM corrects a 24-28% interfacial conductance underestimation in Au/Si, recovers intrinsic silica conductivity in Au/Ti/SiO$_2$, and eliminates a 40% cross-plane conductivity underestimation in Au/MoS$_2$. In bimetallic Au/Ti/Si stacks, where all three non-classical mechanisms act simultaneously, nonlocal modeling reconciles the $116$-$137$ W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ local-fit scatter across spot sizes and frequency windows into a configuration-independent intrinsic silicon conductivity of $141$ W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. For ion-irradiated and graded media with continuous conductivity profiles, PRISM can autonomously construct and verify a deep operator network solver to reconstruct steep damage gradients. By uniting non-equilibrium transport physics and identifiability screening with autonomous model synthesis, PRISM establishes a generalizable paradigm readily extensible to broader optothermal and thermal-wave metrology modalities.
item.dc:creator: Yicong Qiu, Ziyang Zhong, Ziyan Qian, Yang Lu, Yong Jian Hong, Chenhan Liu, Qiye Zheng

item.title: Which Adiabatic Cycles Alter an Action Variable?
item.description: arXiv:2610.40671v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Action variables are adiabatic invariants: their values are preserved during adiabatic time evolutions in completely integrable classical Hamiltonian systems. Nevertheless, an adiabatic cycle can alter how an action variable depends on phase-space variables that are independent of adiabatic parameters. Such a change, which we call action variable holonomy, induces adiabatic torus pumping in phase space. For a family of completely integrable kicked-top systems, a homotopy classification of adiabatic cycles identifies which adiabatic cycles induce action variable holonomy and adiabatic torus pumping. A physical example is also provided.
item.dc:creator: Atushi Tanaka, Taksu Cheon

item.title: Analog and hybrid computing in the 21st century
item.description: arXiv:2611.00446v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Analog computers solve problems through physical representations of mathematical variables and relations, often using the dynamics of electronic circuits and their associated signals. Many analog computers directly represent nonlinear dynamical systems; they encode their solutions in the signals that they generate. Although most modern scientific computing relies on digital architectures with inherently discrete-valued representations and algorithmic approaches, the design constraints of such architectures increasingly limit both performance and energy efficiency. Analog systems can circumvent some of these constraints; they execute specific computations very efficiently by mapping them directly onto physical processes using smaller and simpler computing elements than the ones in digital architectures. In this article, we provide an interdisciplinary perspective on modern analog and hybrid (i.e., analog-digital) computing. We discuss how modern scientific computing workflows can leverage analog approaches in various applications, such as in simulating dynamical systems, performing optimization, and enabling more energy-efficient implementations of artificial intelligence.

item.title: Nonlinear Physics and Self-Organized Criticality in Astrophysics
item.description: arXiv:2611.01119v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The definition of self-organized criticality (SOC) is ambiguous and controversial. Here we discuss the nonlinear physics of six basic SOC definitions, such as: phase transitions, fractal structures, power laws, SOC contingency, exponential growth, and diffusive decay. Statistics of SOC events or avalanche processes can be inferred from their size distributions, or from their spatio-temporal evolution.
item.dc:creator: Markus J. Aschwanden

item.title: Persistence of Fractal Structures in Iterated Quantum Protocols: Robustness to Preparation and Gate Errors
item.description: arXiv:2611.01238v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Repeatedly combining entangling gates on an ensemble of qubits with measurement and postselection on a part of them induces a nonlinear evolution of the unmeasured qubits' state, whose fractal convergence boundaries make the outcome sensitive to the initial state. We study a family of iterated protocols in which $n$ identical qubits are coupled by CNOT gates, $n-1$ of them are postselected, and a parametrized single-qubit unitary acts on the survivor. For orders $n=2$ to $5$, we map the box-counting dimension of the pure-state Julia sets over the complex parameter plane and identify the symmetries that constrain it. Allowing mixed initial states, we find that moderate preparation noise preserves the main parameter-dependent trends of the boundary dimension over much of the studied range, and that the three-dimensional quasi-Julia boundary in the Bloch ball has a dimension that is approximately equal to the dimension of the pure-state Julia set plus one. We further model gate imperfections by an effective depolarizing channel and by fixed coherent interactions. Weak errors leave the estimated dimensions consistent with their ideal values even where the convergence regions visibly deform, and $ZZ$ errors are shown to be exactly conjugate to the ideal protocol at a rotated parameter. Finally, we analyze the postselection and storage cost of an implementation and propose a diagnostic test combining conditional fidelity with acceptance statistics, which we demonstrate on IQM Emerald and Rigetti Cepheus-1-108Q.
item.dc:creator: Attila Portik, Orsolya K\'alm\'an, Tam\'as Kiss

item.title: Chaos, Fractals, and Ergodicity in Nonlinear Quantum Protocols
item.description: arXiv:2611.01249v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Iterated nonlinear quantum protocols provide a straightforward way of realizing nonlinear dynamics in quantum systems through measurement and postselection. We investigate a family of protocols in which the order of the induced nonlinearity is controlled by the number of qubits involved in a single step. By examining the resulting rational maps and applying a set of numerical diagnostics, we identify extended parameter regions that exhibit ergodic-like dynamics for protocol orders $n=3,4,$ and $5$. We further characterize the associated chaotic behavior through the distribution of Lyapunov exponents. Our results show that ergodic-like dynamics persists beyond the quadratic case, while the geometry of the corresponding parameter regions and the typical degree of chaoticity depend strongly on the order of the nonlinear transformation.
item.dc:creator: Attila Portik, Orsolya K\'alm\'an, Tam\'as Kiss

item.title: Fractal Period Locking and Action-Quantized Resonances in the Open Quantum Baker Map
item.description: arXiv:2610.23573v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We open the quantum baker map with a position window of width $w$ and center $q_c$. Classical pruning tiles the $(q_c,w)$ plane into diamonds where the $T$ leading resonances form root-of-unity multiplets. At $w=1/2$ one periodic orbit survives for almost every $q_c$, and the multiplets are quantized without free parameters: their modulus $2^{-1/2}$ saturates the pressure bound and their phase is the orbit action. The multiplets form cycling multicomponent cat states. Finally, the opening reduces to one flag qubit per step, and on an IBM superconducting processor the return probability already revives at the period selected by the window.
item.dc:creator: Leonardo Ermann

item.title: Reservoir as a Dynamical System: A Tutorial Review
item.description: arXiv:2610.32421v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This brief tutorial review examines the operation of reservoir computing from the standpoint of nonlinear dynamics and provides a concise overview of recent advances in the field. We begin by delineating the predictive capabilities of reservoir systems, followed by a succinct yet sufficient introduction to the nonlinear dynamical systems techniques that will be employed throughout this article to elucidate reservoir functioning. Subsequently, we describe reservoir operation using these techniques in the context of successful prediction, accompanied by all necessary implementation codes. The objective of this article is to offer a practical guide to the implementation of reservoir computing while, from a nonlinear dynamics perspective, explaining the mechanisms by which reservoirs achieve accurate predictions.
item.dc:creator: Sarika Jalan, Ling Feng, Dishant Sisodia, Kohei Nakajima

item.title: Periodic orbits underlying optical turbulence in the Lugiato-Lefever equation
item.description: arXiv:2509.10283v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Optical turbulence in driven nonlinear resonators is a form of spatiotemporal chaos that remains poorly understood and is largely characterized through simulations and experiments but lacks a dynamical-systems description. Here we show that in the regime of weak spatiotemporal chaos, the dynamics is structured by families of exact, fully nonlinear, time-periodic solutions of the Lugiato-Lefever equation for driven-dissipative Kerr resonators. These unstable periodic orbits, which we term Oscillating Turing Rolls (OTR), are embedded within the spatiotemporal chaos of optical turbulence. Parametric continuation using Newton-Krylov methods reveals their existence range, stability, and bifurcation-theoretic origin. In symmetry-constrained domains, OTR solutions are intermittently shadowed by chaotic trajectories; in extended domains, they appear as localized motifs of spatiotemporal chaos. Identifying these nonlinear, non-chaotic building blocks establishes a dynamical-systems-based description of optical turbulence in nonlinear optical resonators.
item.dc:creator: Andrey Gelash, Savyaraj Deshmukh, Andrey Shusharin, Tobias M. Schneider, Tobias J. Kippenberg

item.title: A Mathematical Framework for Linear Response Theory for Nonautonomous Systems
item.description: arXiv:2603.19509v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Linear Response theory aims to predict how added forcing alters the statistical properties of a system. This has been predominantly studied for autonomous dynamical systems, yet many systems in the physical, natural, and social sciences are inherently nonautonomous. In such settings, one would like to understand how the system's time-dependent statistical properties change when additional infinitesimal forcings are applied. This question is of clear practical relevance, but from a rigorous mathematical viewpoint it has been addressed only for a few specific classes of systems and perturbations. Here we provide a rigorous linear response theory for a rather general class of deterministic and random nonautonomous systems satisfying a specific set of assumptions that are the counterpart of the standard assumptions used in the autonomous setting. A central ingredient is rapid loss of memory along the nonautonomous evolution. Our main strategy is to reformulate the sequential dynamics as a fixed-point problem for a global transfer operator acting on an extended sequence space of measures. This yields explicit and readily implementable causal response formulas for predicting the effect of small perturbations on time-dependent statistical states. We illustrate the theory on two representative classes: sequential compositions of expanding maps and sequential compositions of noisy random maps. We also establish linear response for reflected Euler-Maruyama discretizations of dissipative nonautonomous stochastic differential equations with nondegenerate additive Gaussian noise, on fixed compact domains. As a physical application, we study the response of a Ghil-Sellers climate energy balance model, discretized in latitude and time to a time-dependent perturbation of the greenhouse parameter.
item.dc:creator: Stefano Galatolo, Valerio Lucarini

item.title: Same worst case, different risk: how transient response shapes failure probability
item.description: arXiv:2606.00789v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The smallest disturbance that can push a dynamical system into failure is a standard measure of stability, but it does not determine how likely failure is under randomly directed disturbances of a given size. The geometry of the transient response connects the two. In the linearized dynamics, each failure boundary and each time after the disturbance define a response vector along the most damaging disturbance. The convex hull of these vectors, the response hull, determines the linear failure-probability curve through its support function. The longest vector sets the worst-case threshold. The mean and spread of the support function set where the curve rises and how steeply, but the mean does not rank systems by risk in general. Under mild regularity conditions, an exact linear-response relation shows how a parameter change shifts the disturbance size at which a given fraction fails: through the mean susceptibility of the directions on that threshold. For weakly damped oscillators, the susceptibility to damping is approximately proportional to the time of a direction's dominant response. Damping thus acts mainly on late failure routes rather than on the early one that sets the worst case, changing the failure probability substantially while barely moving the worst-case threshold. At fixed power imbalance, lowering the inertia instead nearly rescales the hull, moving worst case and risk together. In benchmark power-grid models, the linear predictions agree closely with nonlinear simulations. Strong nonlinear coupling, invisible to linear response, can break this picture; we show how it enters at second order.
item.dc:creator: Surachate Limkumnerd

item.title: One Shot, Twenty-One Balls: A Computer-Assisted Proof of a Single-Stroke Total Clearance in an Idealized Model of Snooker
item.description: arXiv:2607.12995v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Snooker folklore holds that no single stroke can pocket all twenty-one object balls. We examine the claim in an explicit model: twenty-two equal disks on a rectangle with six pocket points, under constant rolling deceleration, frictionless collisions with normal restitution, and lossy specular cushions. We exhibit a configuration and a stroke, and prove in interval arithmetic that every stroke in an explicit box around it pockets all twenty-one object balls, so the set of successful strokes has positive measure. That set is a ribbon: every speed from 9.3213 to 12 m/s works, while the certified window of directions is 9.4813e-43 radians wide, a number explained by a first-order analysis of twenty near-grazing collisions. A second configuration, a near-frozen cluster, has a certified window 9.4e-4 radians wide, thirty-nine orders of magnitude wider; its certificate uses Taylor models of degree six. The strokes with a given list of events form a semialgebraic set, and the endpoints of the windows are algebraic numbers. For the regulation opening position we state the corresponding conjecture, and show that if it holds with a regular witness then a finite certified search establishes it.
item.dc:creator: Avner Kantor
